summary:
Sky Explorer is a public-facing web platform that makes NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations accessible to citizen scientists, enabling users of all experience levels to explore the sky and investigate astronomical changes over time.

SPHEREx observes the sky across 102 near-infrared spectral bands, offering opportunities to identify moving objects and variable stars. However, its enormous dataset and differences in observation conditions make direct comparisons challenging.

Sky Explorer addresses these challenges through two complementary features.

The Sky Viewer provides an interactive, all-sky infrared map where users can pan, zoom, switch wavelengths, search by object name or coordinates, and explore random locations.

The Blink Viewer retrieves observations of selected regions from different epochs. A wavelength-matching algorithm identifies comparable infrared passbands, while image alignment keeps stationary features consistent. Users can blink between observations to detect movement or brightness changes.

Sky Explorer also introduces community-driven review, allowing users to flag unusual features for others to assess. Promising findings can be escalated for scientific follow-up, while known objects and imaging artefacts can be ruled out.

By combining accessible visualisation, automated data processing and collaborative investigation, Sky Explorer lowers barriers to citizen science and empowers the public to contribute to astronomical discovery.
details:
1. Interactive Sky Exploration

Sky Explorer's main interface is an interactive infrared sky map built using Aladin Lite, an astronomical visualisation tool developed by the Centre de Données astronomiques de Strasbourg (CDS).

The viewer displays NASA's SPHEREx Data Release 1 (DR1) all-sky spectral cube through the Hierarchical Progressive Survey (HiPS) format. This allows users to explore the sky through progressively loaded image tiles, similar to the navigation experience of Google Maps.

Users can navigate by panning and zooming, entering Right Ascension (RA) and declination (Dec) coordinates, searching for astronomical objects by name, or selecting a random sky location. Coordinates can be entered in decimal degrees or sexagesimal notation.

The interface also provides positional information, including celestial coordinates and constellation identification. For citizen scientists unfamiliar with astronomy, particularly the RA/Dec coordinate system, displaying the constellation name provides a recognisable celestial reference. This helps users develop a sense of where they are looking in the night sky, making astronomical exploration more intuitive and accessible.

Users can switch between the available infrared wavelength channels from SPHEREx's 102-band spectral survey to examine how astronomical structures appear at different wavelengths.

Object-name resolution and nearby-object information are supported by external astronomical services, including CDS Sesame and SIMBAD.

As NASA releases additional SPHEREx observations, Sky Explorer is designed to incorporate these datasets, expanding the number of available observation epochs. This will eventually allow users to blink between more than two frames, providing a more detailed view of how astronomical objects move or vary over time.

2. Scientific Investigation Using the Blink Viewer

When users select a location and choose Analyze Area, Sky Explorer opens its Blink Viewer to investigate how that region has changed over time.

The backend queries NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) using the International Virtual Observatory Alliance's Simple Image Access (SIA 2.0) protocol.

The query returns metadata describing available SPHEREx observations, including their timestamps, detector identifiers, sky footprints and download locations.

Sky Explorer then identifies suitable observations from different epochs, prioritising those with comparable infrared wavelengths and sufficient spatial coverage.

Unlike ordinary photographs, SPHEREx observations cannot always be compared directly. Differences in telescope orientation and the position-dependent wavelengths of its linear variable filters can cause the same astronomical object to be recorded at different wavelengths.

Our backend therefore implements a wavelength-aware observation-selection algorithm.

3. Wavelength-Matching Algorithm

SPHEREx uses six detector arrays equipped with linear variable filters (LVFs). The effective wavelength recorded at a particular sky position depends on where that position falls within the detector image.

Consequently, observations of the same coordinates at different times may sample different infrared wavelengths. Comparing them without accounting for this difference could introduce apparent brightness changes unrelated to genuine astronomical variability.

To address this, Sky Explorer estimates the wavelength corresponding to the target coordinates for each candidate observation.

First, the backend uses the observation's sky-footprint polygon, supplied in the SIA metadata, to estimate the orientation and location of the detector image.

The polygon's corner coordinates are projected onto a local celestial coordinate plane and used to construct an approximate transformation between sky coordinates and detector pixel coordinates.

Next, the target's estimated detector position is combined with the detector-specific wavelength calibration to calculate its approximate central wavelength and bandwidth.

This process allows the backend to evaluate and rank numerous candidate observations without first downloading every FITS image. Downloading hundreds of full observations for comparison could take many minutes or even hours, making such an approach impractical for an interactive web application. By estimating wavelengths directly from metadata, Sky Explorer significantly reduces unnecessary data transfers and allows users to retrieve suitable observations much more efficiently.

Observations are grouped by epoch and compared using wavelength compatibility, bandwidth similarity and other selection criteria. The backend prioritises suitable observation pairs from the same detector array.

Once a pair is selected, its actual wavelengths are verified using the spatial World Coordinate System (WCS) and wavelength calibration contained in the downloaded FITS files.

Experimental Validation

We validated this metadata-only wavelength-prediction method using SPHEREx D3 and D5 observations from May and December 2025.

Across 40 tested positions, the maximum wavelength-prediction errors were approximately 3.59 nm for D3 and 2.74 nm for D5.

For our M101 test field, the algorithm predicted a wavelength difference of 16.20 nm between two selected observations. Subsequent calculations using their downloaded FITS files gave an actual difference of 16.78 nm.

These results demonstrate the feasibility of using observation metadata to efficiently shortlist wavelength-compatible images.

4. Field of View and Spatial Coverage

Users can select a scientific field of view (FOV) between 0.02° and 0.5°, with a default of 0.1°.

Before downloading images, the backend checks whether the requested region can be accommodated within each candidate observation's usable footprint.

A provisional 20-pixel boundary margin helps account for uncertainty in the approximate coordinate transformation and reduces the risk of selecting observations too close to detector edges.

The backend also supports rotating the requested field in 15° increments to identify orientations that provide sufficient coverage across both observations. A north-up orientation is preferred where possible.

Candidate pairs that cannot accommodate the requested region are rejected.

5. FITS Processing and Image Alignment

After selecting an observation pair, Sky Explorer retrieves calibrated SPHEREx Level 2 FITS cutouts from IRSA.

The downloaded regions include additional surrounding image data to support reprojection and avoid missing pixels around the edges of the final field.

Each FITS image contains calibrated infrared measurements and associated metadata, including spatial WCS information, wavelength calibration, quality flags and variance data.

The backend uses Astropy and astronomical image-reprojection techniques to align the observations onto a common celestial coordinate grid.

This is essential because the original images may have different telescope orientations. Without alignment, stationary stars and other astronomical features would appear to shift between frames, potentially producing false indications of movement.

SPHEREx observations also contain quality flags indicating potential instrumental effects, such as saturation, transient detector events and processing errors. Rather than automatically hiding every flagged pixel, Sky Explorer adopts a visualisation-oriented approach.

Because blinking is primarily a visual technique for identifying positional and brightness changes, we retain pixels carrying flags such as OVERFLOW, SUR_ERROR, TRANSIENT and BLOOM, provided their image values can be displayed. Masking these pixels could otherwise produce large transparent regions in the cores of bright stars, making them appear unnatural and potentially distracting citizen scientists from recognising genuine changes.

Only pixels flagged as NONFUNC (permanently unusable) or MISSING_DATA are explicitly excluded by the quality-flag policy. Additional invalid numerical measurements may also be excluded during processing. The original quality information is retained so that users can distinguish potentially unreliable measurements from genuine astronomical signals.

The resulting aligned images are converted into display-ready frames while retaining their observation metadata.

6. Blink Viewer and Visual Investigation

The aligned images are displayed sequentially in the Blink Viewer, allowing users to identify positional changes or variations in brightness.

Users can pause or resume playback, step between observations, adjust the blinking speed and zoom into the displayed images.

The interface also provides observation information, including dates, wavelengths, detector details and coverage information.

By automatically aligning observations and prioritising wavelength compatibility, Sky Explorer reduces the manual processing required to compare infrared observations.

Nevertheless, apparent changes are not automatically interpreted as astronomical discoveries. Instrumental artefacts, noise, differences in spectral response and other observational effects can also produce apparent variability.

7. Community Review and Citizen Science

Sky Explorer incorporates a community-review concept designed to encourage collaborative investigation of unusual astronomical features.

When a user notices something unusual, they can select Flag for Review.

The user is prompted to provide a title and brief description, and to mark the location of the suspected anomaly in the relevant observation frames. This preserves the context needed for subsequent review.

Other citizen scientists can then examine the flagged observations and select one of three responses:

  • Warrants Further Investigation
  • Likely Imaging Artefact or Known Source
  • Uncertain

The proposed review system requires at least five independent assessments, with at least 80% recommending further investigation, before a report is escalated to the Sky Explorer Team.

Reports passing this threshold would undergo manual scientific checks, potentially including catalogue cross-matching, examination of quality flags and comparison against additional observations.

Where appropriate, sufficiently validated observations of Solar System minor bodies could be prepared for submission to the Minor Planet Center (MPC). Other types of astronomical phenomena would require different follow-up channels.

The current community-review implementation is a browser-local demonstration using simulated accounts and review progression. Cross-user synchronisation, real notifications and external scientific submissions are intended future extensions.

8. NASA Datasets and Supporting Technologies

NASA SPHEREx DR1 All-Sky Spectral Cube

The primary visualisation dataset is the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky spectral cube, accessed through IRSA's HiPS image service.

It provides the infrared imagery used in the interactive sky viewer and allows users to explore the available wavelength channels.

Source: https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/data/hips/SPHEREx/spherex_allsky_cube

NASA SPHEREx DR1 Level 2 Calibrated Observations

The Blink Viewer uses timestamped, calibrated SPHEREx Level 2 FITS observations retrieved from IRSA.

These provide the spatially resolved infrared measurements, observation timestamps, wavelength calibration and quality information needed for comparisons between different epochs.

Source: https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/

The IRSA SIA 2.0 service is used for observation discovery, while IRSA's image-access service provides the FITS data.

Software and Supporting Services

Sky Explorer uses React and TypeScript for its interactive frontend, FastAPI and Python for backend processing, and Aladin Lite for sky visualisation.

Astronomical calculations and image processing use libraries including Astropy, NumPy, SciPy and Reproject.

CDS Sesame and SIMBAD provide supporting astronomical name resolution and catalogue information.

The platform uses real SPHEREx observations rather than synthetic astronomical images.

9. Development and Future Improvements

The present prototype demonstrates interactive infrared sky exploration, automated observation selection, wavelength-aware matching, FITS retrieval, image alignment and visual blinking.

Further development will focus on extending and validating the system across additional sky regions, detectors and survey releases, improving quality-flag inspection, and supporting a genuinely shared citizen-science review platform.

We also intend to introduce educational guides to help users understand the astronomical phenomena they may encounter. These would explain the scientific principles behind apparent motion, including stellar proper motion and parallax, as well as brightness variability in stars and other astronomical objects. Illustrated examples of genuine astronomical changes and common instrumental artefacts would help citizen scientists recognise features worth investigating while reducing false-positive reports.

Another planned enhancement is the integration of complementary astronomical surveys, including optical observations from Pan-STARRS and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), astrometric information from Gaia, and historical infrared observations from NASA's WISE mission.

Comparing observations across different wavelength ranges and instruments can provide complementary evidence about an astronomical source. For example, an unusual feature detected in SPHEREx infrared imagery could be compared against optical observations or historical infrared data to help distinguish genuine astronomical phenomena from wavelength-dependent emission, known objects or instrumental artefacts. Such comparisons would provide additional context and strengthen the assessment of candidate discoveries, although differences in observation dates, sensitivity and spectral response must also be considered.

Other potential enhancements include multi-wavelength image combinations, spectral analysis, more sophisticated moving-object identification and improved mechanisms for coordinating scientific follow-up.

10. Use of Super Intelligence

Generative artificial intelligence tools, including ChatGPT and coding assistants, were used to assist with brainstorming, scientific workflow development, software implementation, debugging and documentation.

The resulting methods and code were evaluated through testing with real SPHEREx observations. Astronomical image data were obtained from the cited archives rather than generated by AI.
